text: Most people meet ServiceNow through Incident Management — logging a ticket when a laptop won't connect to VPN, assigning it to a queue, tracking it until it's resolved. That's IT Service Management, ITSM: Incident, Problem, Change, and Request Management. It's the oldest part of the product and still what most organizations buy first. But calling ServiceNow "the ITSM tool" is a bit like calling a smartphone "the phone app" — technically where most people start, but nowhere near the whole thing.

ServiceNow's own name for the underlying product is the Now Platform. ITSM is just one application built on top of it. So is ITOM, IT Operations Management, covering discovery, the CMDB, and event management. So is ITBM for project and portfolio tracking, HR Service Delivery for employee case management, Customer Service Management for external support, Security Operations for incident and vulnerability response, Source-to-Pay for procurement, and thousands of custom scoped applications that companies and partners build entirely from scratch.

None of those products required ServiceNow to invent a new engine underneath them. Each ships as its own licensed product with its own tables and its own place in the navigation, but every one of them runs on the exact same platform underneath Incident Management.

Here's the fact this entire course is built around: Incident Management itself is just an application. The incident table is a database table like any other. Its form is built with the same Form Designer used for a custom HR case or a company's own in-house vehicle-tracking app. The logic that auto-assigns an incident runs on the same Business Rules and Client Scripts engine available to any developer building anything else on the instance.

That's why job postings say ServiceNow Administrator or ServiceNow Developer, almost never ITSM Administrator. The market already treats this as a transferable platform skill — tables, forms, workflow, and scripting that carry across ITSM, HR, CSM, and whatever custom applications a given employer happens to run.

Learn the platform once, and you can read, administer, and eventually build almost anything on ServiceNow, regardless of which specific product line it ships under. Next up: how that one platform actually gets split into separate instances for development, testing, and production.
